output.headline: Macron welcomes Burnham's openness to UK rejoining the EU
output.bodyHtml:
In a major boost to supporters of rejoining, Emmanuel Macron welcomed Andy Burnham’s comments on Wednesday. “Welcome back,” the French president said in English at a press conference in Madrid.

He continued in French: “If the British want to come back and if the prime minister is moving in that direction, I think that is very good news, both for his country and for the Europeans.”

An EU spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and valued partner of the European Union. It is for the UK government to set out how it wishes to develop its relationship with the EU going forward. We remain open to engaging on the options it may put forward.”

Senior Downing Street officials have been reaching out to thinktanks and pollsters as they test public support for the UK rejoining the EU.

Aides to Andy Burnham have been talking to EU experts in a range of organisations about how the public would view a promise to rejoin, as momentum builds behind including such a pledge in the next Labour manifesto.

Some in No 10 are keen to promise that Labour would at least negotiate over re-entry to the bloc, something Burnham has previously said he wants to see happen “in his lifetime”. Others are nervous, however, that making such a promise could revive the flagging political fortunes of Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader.

Burnham used his first Labour conference speech as leader to announce a review of the options for Britain’s relationship with Europe, and added on Wednesday that these options should include rejoining entirely.

The prime minister told delegates on Tuesday: “Brexit has done more harm than good. So I will take the opportunity around the [UK-EU] summit to lay out to you, to lay out to the country, what I believe are the different options for Britain’s long-term relationship with our European partners.”

On Wednesday he clarified that this would include an option to rejoin – something ruled out by his predecessor Keir Starmer.

Burnham told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “We could stay as we are. That’s definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay. We could look at what [the former Conservative chancellor] George Osborne has said about a customs union, we could look at what the Liberal Democrats said at their conference about the single market, or we could go all the way.”

Related: Andy Burnham wants to review the UK’s relationship with the EU. What are the options?

Pro-EU campaigners welcomed Burnham’s comments, arguing that rejoining is the best way to boost UK growth rates, while political opponents reacted with outrage.

Alex Burghart, the Conservative deputy leader, said: “Labour cannot blame a democratic vote from over a decade ago for the consequences of their own economic decisions.”

The Guardian has learned that Burnham’s comments are part of a wider effort by No 10 to test consensus over rejoining, with a view to possibly including such a promise in the next manifesto.

Officials have been in talks with several prominent thinktanks and pollsters, who have been working on projects to flesh out arguments over rejoining and test public opinion.

Last week, the Tony Blair Institute released a paper arguing that Burnham should seek talks with Brussels over becoming a member once more but should only do so if Europe relaxed its regulations in sectors including energy and technology.

On the same day, the pro-EU campaign group Best for Britain released a megapoll conducted by YouGov suggesting Labour could more than double its seat total if it went into the next election promising to rejoin.

Over the coming weeks, the influential Institute for Public Policy Research will release a paper calling for the country to rejoin, while Think Labour has also been looking into how difficult it would be to do so.

Some in Downing Street are buoyed up by polling which shows that promising to re-enter the bloc does little to boost support for Reform. They also point out that Farage attacked the prime minister’s speech for the promise to change the pensions triple lock, rather than his comments about Europe.

The Guardian has been told that some at the top of government wanted the prime minister to use this week’s speech to promise to begin work on rejoining after the next election, rather than carrying out a review.

In the end, such an option was ruled out because the party was already bracing itself for a fight over pensions and did not want to give succour to Farage while he faces accusations about millions of pounds’ worth of donations to his party.

No 10 said the prime minister did not ever consider making such a promise in the speech and that it was not included in any draft of it.

Some believe it would be difficult to persuade Brussels, which has engaged in multiple rounds of talks about Britain’s relationship with the EU, to embark on negotiations over re-accession.

Burnham’s willingness to look at all options seems to have been accompanied by fresh engagement on the EU’s Made in Europe legislation, which threatens to lock UK goods out of certain supply chains on the continent.

No 10 has sought to have British manufacturers classified as European for the purposes of that legislation, with officials threatening to delay an EU-UK summit until London receives signals that there could be an accommodation.

Since Burnham’s speech, however, there is now talk of holding the summit on 20 November.

One EU diplomat said it was necessary to get Starmer’s old reset agenda concluded before talks of “a real reset” could begin, confirming support for a UK-EU summit as early as possible.

A second diplomat said there was “a good feeling” that Burnham was now looking at all options and seeking a consensus, “something Brussels has wanted to see”.
output.standfirst: Emmanuel Macron has welcomed Andy Burnham's openness to rejoining the EU, as No 10 tests public and diplomatic support for the idea; critics say it could revive Reform UK.
output.progress: No 10 is consulting thinktanks and pollsters on rejoining, and diplomats say there is 'a good feeling' about holding an early UK-EU summit.

output.headline: Crew and passengers team up to save flydubai jet and all 174 aboard
output.bodyHtml:
Bleeding on the floor of the flydubai flight deck, Smit Machchhar managed to click the release to open the cockpit door, letting passengers and crew get in, overpower his attacker and save all 174 people on board.

He had been stabbed moments earlier by his fellow pilot, in an apparent effort to crash the plane as it travelled from Dubai to Tel Aviv. Machchhar, an Indian citizen from Mumbai, is being treated in a hospital in Saudi Arabia’s north-western city of Tabuk, where the plane landed safely.

Several people have been hailed as heroes for helping wrest control of the plane from the attacker who apparently tried to crash it, Machchhar among them, according to Israeli officials, who provided much of the detail on how events played out inside the plane.

In a post on X early on Thursday, Indian prime minister Narendra Modi lauded Machchhar a “hero”.

Related: ‘Whoever is hearing me, we need help’: how flight 1073 survived its 17,000ft plunge

“In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously ‌injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others. His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy,” Modi ​said.

Earlier, Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu had been equally impressed by Machchhar’s actions. “Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker.”

A struggle began when Machchhar’s fellow pilot – reportedly an Omani national – stabbed him, sending the jet plunging nearly 14,000ft (4,267 metres) in less than 30 seconds.

Soon after several passengers were able to enter the cockpit to help subdue the attacker.

“What made it difficult for us was [Machchhar] himself,” said Yaniv Hayoun, who was among those in the cockpit and whom Netanyahu described as a plumber. “He had been stabbed and was on the other side of the door.”

Hayoun later told Netanyahu that as people wrestled with the attacker, “I jumped back, grabbed the controls, and started pulling back the handles”, the way he had seen on television shows. Then other crew members took over.

Dr Shota Musaev, a dentist on board, was also among those who ran to the cockpit. He told CNN they found the attacker on the floor on top of the pilot, stabbing him. He then rushed to help Machchhar, “terrified” he was going to die.

“He was covered in cuts – his head, his hands – they were practically sliced open, almost severed in two … he had lost a lot of blood and was in bad shape.

“I think that if we had waited even a few more moments, we would have lost him; his blood pressure had plummeted, he suddenly lost consciousness, and there was blood everywhere,” he said.

Musaev told CNN he also helped subdue the attacker, recalling that he tied him up using headphone cords and plastic zipties.

Other crew members then stabilised the descent of the plane and began to land it safely in north-western Saudi Arabia. Among those who intervened was an off-duty British pilot, according to a passenger, Almog Itali, who said the plane was carrying a pair of relief pilots who were meant to fly the next flight.

“The relief pilots are European, one of them British, who entered [the cockpit] and pulled the aircraft up, pulled the yoke, stabilised the plane and landed us in Saudi Arabia,” Itali said in a clip posted by the BBC. Other reports suggested the off-duty pilots were from South Africa or New Zealand.

Indian media reported that Machchhar underwent surgery in Saudi Arabia, while Indian officials say he is in a stable condition. They say they have been in touch with his family – reportedly a wife and two children – who live in Dubai.

Aviation experts have expressed surprise the plane did not crash after a descent so extreme that most of the rudder was ripped off the tail. One passenger described the moment of the nosedive as like “massive turbulence … for 20 or 30 seconds.”

“That was a serious descent and strong aerodynamic forces on that rudder for that to happen. I’m just amazed the aircraft didn’t come apart,” said former United Airlines pilot and aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo.

“What saved them is there was enough altitude left for them to recover,” said Guzzetti, another aviation expert, who said it may not have been possible for the plane to level out if it had fallen below 10,000 feet.

The fact Machchhar was able to unlock the cockpit door, allowing other passengers to enter and take control of the aircraft, no doubt saved all the passengers on board. Philip Kean the chief executive of Mainland Air in New Zealand – where Machchhar trained for 18 months in 2008 and 2009 – said the pilot had shown leadership after being attacked in mid-air.

Calling Machchhar an above average pilot, Kean told New Zealand publication Stuff that pilots trained for all eventualities, but that managing it successfully when it happens in reality was a “whole different story”.
output.standfirst: A stabbed pilot's swift action let off-duty pilots, a plumber and a dentist overpower his attacker and bring the stricken flydubai jet safely down in Saudi Arabia, saving everyone on board.
output.progress: Off-duty pilots, a plumber and a dentist rushed into the cockpit, subdued the attacker and helped land the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.

output.headline: Security services had advance knowledge of Fairford incident, officials indicate
output.bodyHtml:
There are “strong indications” that Iran played a role in events in which five men were arrested near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire as part of a terror investigation, Andy Burnham has said.

UK officials and Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, have indicated that security services were aware in advance of what was happening.

A statement from Britain’s head of counter-terrorism police hinted that officers swooped on the rural location for several reasons.

Assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor said: “A police response was activated in the early hours of Sunday morning due to a range of information received, including a call from a member of the public about several vehicles acting suspiciously close to RAF Fairford.”

Speaking to the media at the end of the Labour party conference in Liverpool, Burnham said he could not give any more details amid a police investigation, but that Iran was believed to be involved.

On Tuesday, Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, said Washington believed “a foreign actor” was involved in the events on Sunday night at the airbase, which has been used by US planes for missions against Iran.

In an interview with BBC News, Burnham said: “There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex, and serious police investigation.

“And of course, we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America. So it’s ongoing.”

Noting that he had held a meeting of the government’s Cobra emergency committee while in Liverpool, Burnham said: “We are on top of it in every possible way imaginable.”

He added: “We will say more in due course, but we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part.”

Asked why he believed this, Burnham replied: “Well I can’t go into all of those details, but obviously I wouldn’t say it lightly.”

In a separate interview with Sky News, Burnham was asked if he needed to recall parliament, which is in recess for the party conference season. He replied: “At this stage there is not an urgent need to do that, but should that arise, of course, I wouldn’t hesitate.”

The five men, all in their 20s and from London, were arrested in the Gloucestershire countryside near the airbase after a local woman driving home saw a series of vans and men in masks, and called police.

They were first arrested on explosives charges and then later for preparing acts of terrorism. All five were released on police bail on Monday after an examination of what was found in the vans, and searches of addresses linked to them across London.

On Tuesday the Guardian reported increasing confidence of an Iranian link to the weekend’s events.

The decision to release the men has prompted criticism from the Trump administration, with Rubio saying he was “disturbed” by it.

Questioned by the BBC about US criticism of the bail decision, Burnham said this had happened only with very strict conditions.

He said: “I think people need to understand that when it says released, that isn’t as people might think. It’s obviously with the strictest possible bail conditions. We’ve been talking to counterparts in the United States all week to explain what is happening here, how things are being done. I have complete confidence in the way British security services are handling this.”

It emerged on Tuesday that one of the five men arrested called the police to report the incident.

The local woman who also phoned police subsequently told newspapers that she was alarmed the men had been allowed to get so close to the airbase without apparently being noticed.
output.standfirst: Security services had advance knowledge of the Fairford incident, officials say, even as Andy Burnham says Iran is strongly suspected of a role; five men have been bailed under strict conditions.
output.progress: Police have made arrests, convened a Cobra meeting and are working closely with US counterparts on the investigation.

output.headline: Minister says Garvaghy Road resolution is 'tantalisingly close' after marathon talks
output.bodyHtml:
Chris Bryant, the Northern Ireland secretary, said an end to the dispute was “tantalisingly close”, as the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition signalled it would accept a document setting out a resolution if the Orange Order also did so.

Breandán Mac Cionnaith, the leader of the nationalist group, said on Wednesday afternoon that he had been through the document drawn up by Bryant and his team.

“Obviously, I can’t divulge what is in it,” he said after a meeting with Bryant. “But if it’s accepted by the Orange Order, it will be accepted by us.”

Talks to end the Drumcree parade dispute are on a knife-edge, however, after Jamie Bryson, the legal adviser of the Orange Order, said it would “not surrender” to the deal proposed by Bryant.

With echoes of the former Democratic Unionist leader Ian Paisley’s “no surrender” mantra of the 1980s, Bryson told supporters in Portadown that Bryant could keep his deal.

He said he had the authority of the Orange Order’s district master to say: “The Portadown District will not surrender the fundamental principle, not now, not last week, not next week, not ever – ever.”

Bryson said the Portadown Orangemen would not “sell out” even if they were offered £20m.

Government sources said they expected talks to continue on Thursday and possibly into Friday.

But after a second meeting with Bryant on Wednesday evening, Bryson rubbished the residents’ leader’s words.

“Do not be panicked by Breandán Mac Cionnaith coming out and saying there is a document on the table. The document can stay on the table because it won’t be accepted by the Portadown District.”

Earlier in the day, Bryant urged parties to “search deep in their souls for another chunk of compromise” to break the deadlock, after meeting with both sides at Hillsborough Castle, just outside Belfast.

On Tuesday, Mac Cionnaith had described mediation over the dispute as “dead in the water”.

Bryant said on Wednesday: “I would just appeal to everybody – including the wider community, not just the people I have been meeting in the room – that people are going to have to search deep in their souls for another chunk of compromise if we’re going to get to a successful long-term resolution of the situation.”

He added that he and his team were “working flat-out to try and get to a successful resolution, and I think that is tantalisingly close if everybody can just go that extra mile”.

Politicians and others had warned that any parade down Garvaghy Road risked returning Northern Ireland to the bleak days of the Troubles.

But on Sunday a court of appeal overturned a high court injunction banning the Orange Order from processing through the mainly nationalist area, leading to a four-day standoff that has heightened sectarian tensions.

Attempts to march down Garvaghy Road were blocked by protesters, and a small group of Orange Order members has remained at Drumcree church, the starting point of the parade, vowing not to leave until the parade goes ahead.

Jon Boutcher, the chief constable of Northern Ireland’s police force, said the protest stopping the parade was unlawful, and that a major criminal investigation into the blockade was under way. He warned that mob rule must not be allowed to win, and that he would continue to seek a way to facilitate the Orange Order march.

The first minister of Northern Ireland, Michelle O’Neill, visited Garvaghy Road on Wednesday, despite accusations by unionist leaders that she had broken the law by supporting protesters when she went there on Sunday.

Asked if she had broken the law, O’Neill said: “I accept that I made a choice, a choice to stand with the residents of the Garvaghy Road. It is a choice I will continue to make.

“This is very clearly a community which feels under siege, a community that has been put in reverse and retraumatised in terms of what happened 28 years ago.”

The parade was given the go-ahead by the Northern Ireland Parades Commission on Friday, ending a 28-year ban on the Orange Order marching in Garvaghy Road. At a special sitting of the high court the next day, Justice Patricia Smyth issued an order temporarily suspending the parade, but that was overturned on appeal in the small hours of Sunday morning.

Critics of the Parades Commission’s decision included the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, who called it “incomprehensible and wrong”, given that the march prompted some of the most serious violence seen in Northern Ireland in the late 1990s – including the murders of three children – and nearly derailed the 1998 peace process.

On Tuesday, the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition lodged a fresh legal challenge against the march, this time arguing the Parades Commission had “materially misdirected itself” by using historical police assessments over the risk of violence as opposed to a future-looking risk assessment.
output.standfirst: Chris Bryant says a deal to end the Garvaghy Road standoff is close, as nationalists signal they would accept it – but Orange Order adviser Jamie Bryson insists Portadown 'will not surrender'.
output.progress: Northern Ireland secretary Chris Bryant is holding talks with both sides at Hillsborough Castle, with a resolution he calls 'tantalisingly close'.

context.text: Despite warnings of a return to the Troubles, earlier confrontations at Drumcree passed off peacefully, with Orange Order members turning back from police lines without violence.

output.headline: Satellite images document scale of destruction across Gaza since ceasefire
output.bodyHtml:
An update to Google Maps shows the extent of the destruction caused during the three-year Gaza war, and the scale of hardship still facing the territory’s 2.3 million inhabitants.

The images were taken in June this year and show further destruction of homes, businesses, places of worship and infrastructure since a fragile ceasefire came into effect almost 12 months ago.

They show huge tented camps lining much of the shoreline, often within a few metres of the sea. Gaza’s once busy main port, now badly damaged and empty of fishing boats, is surrounded by makeshift accommodation. Any available open space in Gaza City is packed with shacks, tents and huts.

The images also show massive damage to northern towns such as Beit Lahiya and Beit Hanoun, as well as the destruction of places of worship such as the Istiqlal mosque in Khan Younis. Major neighbourhoods in Gaza City such as Jabaliya and Shuja’iya, which were targeted in repeated Israeli offensives, are clearly now uninhabitable.

Swaths of rubble are visible in the south of Gaza, where a wide strip appears to have been cleared by Israeli forces along the border with Egypt. The town of Rafah appears to have been almost entirely reduced to rubble and Tel al-Sultan razed to the ground.

More than 2.1 million displaced people are living in tents and temporary shelters in Gaza, where about 82% of structures – roughly 200,000 buildings – have been damaged, with about two-thirds of those destroyed, according to the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, Unrwa.

A recent UN assessment estimated that the number of destroyed structures across Gaza had increased by 9% since the declaration of a ceasefire in October 2025.

“The estimate of the total amount of rubble in Gaza is 61m tonnes. It is approximately 20 times the amount of rubble generated in all wars across the world over the last 18 years,” Jaco Cilliers, the UN Development Programme’s special representative in Palestine told the Guardian last month. The presence of human remains still buried under the rubble remains one of the most urgent humanitarian problems.

More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the start of the war, mostly civilians. The conflict was triggered by a surprise attack by Hamas into Israel in October 2023, in which militants killed about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and took 251 others hostage.
output.standfirst: New Google Maps imagery taken in June shows deepening destruction of homes, mosques and infrastructure across Gaza, where more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed since the war began.

output.headline: Scientists record one-fifth loss of Switzerland's glacier ice in five years
output.bodyHtml:
Switzerland has lost almost one-fifth of its glacier ice in five years, research has found, reshaping an Alpine landscape where big white glaciers have been reduced to moonlike rock deserts, scientists say.

Swiss glaciers shrank by 5.5% in the first eight months of 2026, according to an annual monitoring report, after a summer of scorching heatwaves that followed a winter with little snow. The reduction in ice volume falls just shy of the record set in 2022 and brings the total loss of glacier ice since 2021 to 19.4%.

Matthias Huss, a glaciologist at ETH Zürich and lead author of the report, said many people do not realise how fast glaciers are retreating, or that just one generation ago some now-barren sites used to sit beneath hundreds of metres of ice. The scientists have not yet compiled a formal tally of lost glaciers this year but said they had witnessed the death of a number of small ones.

“I visited one last week and it’s so impressive to stand in this moonlike landscape where there was a big layer of ice – an extensive glacier – just a few years ago,” said Huss. “And now it’s a rock desert where there’s some scattered blocks of old ice still lying around and melting on the hot rocks.”

The report, a collaboration between the Swiss Glacier Monitoring Network and the Swiss Commission for Cryosphere Observation, found the mean thickness of individual glaciers fell by between 2.5 metres and 4 metres in 2026. Huss said scientists were increasingly seeing glaciers collapse from the inside – the result of internal streams beneath the ice that excavate caverns – rather than simply retreating from surface heat.

“You have huge holes like cheese in the middle of the ice that have collapsing roofs,” said Huss. “These are processes that tear the glaciers apart and make them retreat even faster.”

Europe is warming twice as fast as the global average from the heat-trapping effects of fossil fuel pollution and the destruction of nature, with Alpine regions experiencing some of the most dramatic changes.

Analysis published by MeteoSwiss on Tuesday found the summer half-year from April to September was the hottest and driest it had been since records began in 1864. In that time, humanity has filled the atmosphere with 1.8tn tons of carbon dioxide and heated the planet by about 1.4C.

The heat this summer was worse than in 2022 but Swiss ice loss just missed the record-breaking levels set that year. The scientists attributed this to limited deposits of Saharan dust, which foul the snow and prevent it from reflecting sunlight, as well as slightly greater snow cover at the end of winter and more sunlight in the summer.

Huss visited the former Plattalvafirn, or Griess glacier, in September, which used to cover a mountain flank but lost 99% of its area in just 20 years. The glacier was the subject of some of the most detailed monitoring in the world in the 1950s and Huss worked with its data when he was a PhD student.

“What was different at that time, is that the rates of retreat were still kind of at a normal level,” said Huss. “What we are seeing now is a complete explosion of these melt rates, leading to the disintegration of glaciers. They’re really just falling apart.”
output.standfirst: Annual monitoring by Swiss glaciologists found ice volume fell by 5.5% this year alone, bringing losses since 2021 to 19.4%, as Alpine regions warm twice as fast as the global average.

output.headline: Tennessee execution halted as Christa Pike survives and receives hospital care
output.bodyHtml:
Christa Pike was taken to hospital and was still alive following two lethal injections, her lawyers told the BBC on Wednesday evening. One of her attorneys said she was “being provided life-saving measures”.

Tennessee officials were unable to carry out her execution, media witnesses said Wednesday, despite her being administered two doses of a lethal injection drug.

In a press conference, media witnesses described hearing Pike snore 40 minutes after she was administered two doses of pentobarbital. An ambulance pulled up to Riverbend maximum security institution ahead of the press conference, but Pike’s condition is unclear.

Pike’s attorneys have filed an emergency motion to the US supreme court asking to halt and stay the execution, saying she was in “unnecessary agony” and the state is violating her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment.

A Tennessee department of correction spokesperson Dorinda Carter told media witnesses she was unable to immediately provide information about what happened.

Pike was set to be the first woman to be executed in Tennessee in 200 years, after the US supreme court lifted a lower-court ruling that put her execution on pause earlier in the day.

Pike, who was convicted of murder 30 years ago, was initially scheduled to die by lethal injection on Wednesday morning until her execution was halted hours earlier by a federal appeals court.

In a 2-1 ruling, that court said the delay was necessary to assess whether Pike’s allegations of childhood sexual abuse were fully considered at her sentencing. The state governor and the supreme court had earlier refused calls for clemency.

Tennessee’s attorney general immediately appealed the ruling to the supreme court, writing that the 11th-hour stay rewarded “abusive delay tactics by Pike’s attorneys”, according to the Associated Press.

The US supreme court sided with Tennessee in an order signed by justice Brett Kavanaugh.

Justice Sonia Sotomayor, joined by fellow liberal justices Elena Kagan and Kentanji Brown Jackson, dissented from the court’s order “because its decision clears the way for the state to execute Pike before her still-pending legal challenges to her conviction can be properly considered”.

Pike, who is now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend, who was 17 at the time, killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps in 1995.

The case garnered nationwide headlines due to the ages of those involved and the brutality of the murder.

According to prosecutors, Pike was worried Slemmer was trying to take her then boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, away from her. Together, they lured Slemmer into a wooded area behind the agriculture campus steam plant at the University of Tennessee on 12 January 1995. Pike cut Slemmer’s stomach and throat with a box cutter before smashing her head with a rock.

Shipp carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest and Pike later showed a friend a fragment of Slemmer’s skull.

Shipp was convicted of first-degree murder in 1997 and was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole.

Pike has never denied her involvement in Slemmer’s killing and was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.

“I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime,” Pike said in a statement that was included in her clemency petition.

On Saturday, May Martinez, Slemmer’s mother, said she was waiting for Pike’s execution.

“Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run,” Martinez told the Associated Press, adding: “Not a day goes by, or a minute goes by that I do not think about Colleen. Holidays are the worst.”

The Associated Press contributed reporting
output.standfirst: Christa Pike, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of a Knoxville classmate, was still alive and being treated in hospital 40 minutes after Tennessee administered two lethal doses.
output.progress: Doctors are giving Pike life-saving treatment in hospital, while her lawyers press the US supreme court to halt the execution.

output.headline: Oasis win postponement of auction for unheard 90s recordings
output.bodyHtml:
A collection of unheard Oasis recordings, including 63 live shows, hours of rehearsals and candid conversations between Noel and Liam Gallagher, has been pulled from auction after legal action taken by the band.

In September Littleton Auctions in Worcestershire, England, listed the collection made by the band’s former sound engineer, Huw Richards, with a guide price of between £1.2m and £1.6m.

Richards worked with Oasis from the release of their 1994 debut Definitely, Maybe until 2001. The collection of 209 DAT tapes, 73 analogue cassettes and three MiniDiscs were being sold by the sound engineer’s son, Owain Richards.

Related: Oasis announce 2027 tour, including return to Knebworth 30 years after historic concerts

“Littleton Auctions confirms that the Oasis recordings known as The Desk Tapes have been withdrawn from our October 3 auction in light of legal proceedings,” the auction house’s managing director, Ben Homer, told the BBC.

“We are very disappointed that we cannot offer this significant archive as planned.”

In an interview with the Times in September, Owain Richards, also a sound engineer, called the collection “a piece of history”. He said the audio remained in sufficiently good condition, but as Oasis retained the intellectual property rights, the recordings can’t be released by a potential new owner without the band’s cooperation.

“It is true that Oasis have sued me and my father to try to prevent the auction of the tapes made by my father many years ago,” Richards told the BBC on Wednesday.

“We have agreed to postpone the auction [of the tapes] to enable the legal dispute to be resolved either by litigation or otherwise in an orderly way.”

Littleton Auctions will continue with the auction on Saturday, with other music memorabilia up for sale including an original Kangol Oasis tour parka from Richards’ collection, plus signed Nirvana photographs, autographs of two of the Rolling Stones members, and a guitar signed by Brian May.

“The rest of the sale is unaffected and will take place as normal,” said Homer. “We respect the legal process and will make no further comment on the proceedings at this stage.”

Last month, Noel and Liam Gallagher attended the world premiere of documentary film Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger at Venice film festival followed by its UK premiere in London. The band also recently announced its Live ’27 world tour following their successful reunion tour in 2025.

Oasis have been approached for comment.
output.standfirst: The band's legal action has forced Littleton Auctions to withdraw a collection of unheard live shows, rehearsals and candid conversations between Noel and Liam Gallagher, expected to fetch up to £1.6m.
output.progress: Oasis have sued to block the sale, and the auction house has agreed to postpone it while the dispute is resolved.

output.headline: Islanders' crowdfunded dig uncovers major sixth-century monastery on Lismore
output.bodyHtml:
To the residents of the Scottish island of Lismore, population 190, history is never very far away. The tiny island near Oban in Argyll has no high street or even a pub – if islanders want to meet for a coffee, the only place to do so is in the lively Gaelic heritage centre that records the many centuries of community life on the island.

Documentary evidence records that this quiet place was home to a monastic settlement in the sixth century AD, when missionaries from Ireland were first moving into northern Britain to spread Christianity. But apart from a few fragments of an early carved cross, there was almost nothing to see from this period of history – until a group of local people decided to look harder.

Members of the island’s historical society scraped together funding from grants, donations and legacies of locals and a crowdfunding campaign, then commissioned a professional archaeologist, Dr Clare Ellis of Argyll Archaeology, to lead a group of islanders and other volunteers in an excavation on the site of a much later medieval cathedral.

Their “hugely exciting” findings have not only rewritten the story of the island but cast new light on the spread of Christianity in the period, according to archaeologists. What the islanders discovered were extensive burial grounds, decorated stonework and early buildings – all the features belonging to a major sixth-century monastery, comparable to the much better known site of Iona a little to the south-west.

In addition, the excavations uncovered rare evidence of slightly later high-status craftworking, including huge numbers of crucibles which had been used to cast gold and silver. The finds have shown that rather than being a small island church in an overlooked backwater, the monastery of Lios Mór, founded by Saint Mo Luóc or Moluag, was a high-ranking site of international importance, experts say.

To Robert Hay, a retired plant scientist who moved to the island in 2001 and who coordinated the fundraising and volunteer efforts, the experience was thrilling. “We were [excavating] in this really unfavourable, boggy area. To be digging out the best small crucibles ever found in Scotland – it’s extraordinary,” he said.

“The most exciting moment for me was when they were doing the post-excavation analysis and they found that they had been melting gold, copper, silver, and they were making jewellery on our little island in the seventh century.”

While plenty of islanders have an idle interest in its history, a “dynamic minority” of mostly older people had mustered the volunteers and funds to carry out the digs, said Hay. Raising the low five-figure sum needed to pay for it all had been “just a business of getting down to it and organising and so on”, he said. “It was actually a lot easier than what my previous job used to be.”

Gordon Noble, a professor of archaeology at the University of Aberdeen, said the finds were highly significant. “We know about sites like Iona having these very famous monastic sites from this early medieval world. But apart from the association with Moluag and a piece of sculpture from this site, we knew practically nothing really about Lismore. So it was hugely exciting to see the results emerging through the local group’s work with Clare [Ellis] … This was clearly a really important early Christian establishment.”

While professional archaeologists often worked with local people, Noble said, “it’s not always the community themselves coming up with the ideas. Here, it was very much a bottom-up approach of the heritage society coming up with a plan, working with professionals – and lo and behold, what a great series of discoveries they’ve made at the site.”

Hay said he hoped the finds would go some way to restoring the reputation of Moluag, who has long been overshadowed by the more celebrated Saint Columba, the founder of Iona and the subject of an influential ninth-century biography. “Unfortunately, Moluag never had a hagiographer, so his contribution to the evangelisation of Scotland has been very much underestimated,” he said. “So finding his monastic site and [the evidence of metalworking] – it’s all about recalibrating the situation. I think Moluag had a very big impact on the evangelising of Scotland, but unfortunately, he didn’t get his PR right.”

The results of the community excavations will be published in the forthcoming edition of Antiquity.
output.standfirst: Volunteers on the 190-person island of Lismore raised the funds themselves to uncover a high-status monastic site that experts say rewrites the story of early Christianity in Scotland.

output.trail: A British study has found that butterflies' whirring wings and bright patterns help keep them safe from predators.

output.headline: Samba the fugitive capybara still roaming free six months after zoo escape
output.trail: Six months after her unprecedented escape from Marwell zoo, Samba the capybara remains on the lam in the Hampshire countryside, as a dedicated team tries to track her down.

output.headline: Share your experience of buying through help-to-buy
output.trail: We would like to hear from people in England who used the government's previous equity loan scheme to buy their first home about how it worked out.

output.headline: Share how a climate event reshaped your view of the climate crisis
output.trail: Perhaps you lost your home or possessions in a wildfire, or your mountain business has been affected by glacial retreat and snow scarcity.

output.headline: Share your story: no romantic relationship yet at 18-29
output.trail: Whatever the reason, we want to hear from 18 to 29-year-olds who have never had a romantic relationship.

output.headline: Guardian seeks accounts from passengers assaulted on Britain's railways
output.trail: We want to hear from passengers and members of the public after 13,464 assaults were reported on the mainline railway in 2025-26.

output.headline: How flight 1073 survived a 17,000ft dive and a daring rescue
output.trail: On a morning service from Dubai to Tel Aviv, 150 passengers witnessed a cockpit assault and a daring mid-air rescue that brought the plane down safely.

output.headline: More than 60 Labour MPs back youth mobility scheme with EU
output.trail: The MPs have signed a letter calling on Keir Starmer to support time-limited visas letting 18- to 30-year-olds travel freely between the UK and EU.

output.headline: Labour hopes new trade deals can boost growth without rejoining the EU
output.trail: The party hopes new trade arrangements can boost growth, though this will be hard given it has ruled out rejoining the single market and customs union.

output.headline: Ex-health secretaries reject claim that Brexit would help save the NHS
output.trail: Four former Labour health secretaries have rejected the leave campaign's argument, saying the NHS would be starved of resources outside the EU.

output.headline: Burnham focuses on rebuilding EU bridges ahead of von der Leyen meeting
output.trail: The prime minister says his immediate focus is on rebuilding relations with Europe, while not ruling out a Brexit reversal pledge in the next Labour manifesto.

output.headline: Ministers to weigh pros and cons of UK rejoining the EU
output.trail: The prime minister says he is looking at all options, with ministers set to examine what is doable and weigh the pros and cons of rejoining.

output.headline: Streeting and Burnham make the case for reconsidering the UK-EU relationship
output.trail: Labour leadership contender Wes Streeting calls Brexit a 'catastrophic mistake', while Andy Burnham says he sees a long-term case for rejoining the EU.

output.headline: Emergency landing brings Israel-bound jet down safely
output.trail: The plane made an emergency landing after the pilot tried to crash it following an alleged stabbing by the co-pilot, Israel's prime minister said, as officials probe a possible terror attack.

output.headline: First direct commercial flight between Israel and UAE takes off
output.trail: The flight marks the first tangible result of a US-brokered deal to normalise relations between the two countries, Jared Kushner said.

output.headline: Iranian drones strike US embassy in Riyadh amid regional escalation
output.trail: Israel has bombed Tehran and sent troops into southern Lebanon, as Iranian drones hit the US embassy in Riyadh and President Trump says it is too late to talk.

output.headline: US and Israel launch new wave of strikes on Iran
output.trail: President Trump has said he would respond with force 'never seen before' if Iran retaliates, following the death of Khamenei.

output.headline: Trump's Peace review: a fascinating account of upheaval and real progress
output.trail: Barak Ravid has written a fascinating account of four chaotic years in US-Israel policy during which, our reviewer says, some genuine progress was nonetheless made.

output.headline: Trump and Netanyahu score diplomatic moment as UAE, Bahrain and Israel sign accords
output.trail: The three countries signed the agreements at a White House ceremony, seen as an image boost for both Trump and Netanyahu.

output.headline: NI secretary holds talks as nationalists pursue fresh legal challenge
output.trail: The Northern Ireland secretary is holding talks with both sides, even as nationalists say mediation over the Drumcree parade is 'dead in the water' and the Garvaghy Road group launches a fresh legal challenge.

output.headline: Diplomatic mood music shifts as UK and EU seek Northern Ireland deal
output.trail: Talks between the Irish foreign minister and his UK counterpart have been announced as the UK ends its standoff with the EU, amid a change in the diplomatic 'mood music'.

output.headline: Governments hope to defuse Garvaghy Road march standoff
output.trail: The Drumcree dispute shows how Northern Ireland's troubled past can still threaten its peace, and governments are hoping the impasse over the Orange Order's march can be defused.

output.headline: Northern Ireland protocol talks move into final phase, deal possible next week
output.trail: Negotiations have entered a crucial final phase, with Rishi Sunak preparing to hold calls with EU leaders.

output.headline: Eurosceptic lawyers submit fresh proposal on Northern Ireland deal
output.trail: Lawyers advising Tory Eurosceptics have submitted a fresh proposal on Northern Ireland, even as Boris Johnson hints he may not support Rishi Sunak's deal, which the ex-PM calls the best way forward.

output.headline: Gerry Adams wins compensation case after convictions were overturned
output.trail: A judge ruled the former Sinn Féin leader was wrongly denied compensation, a victory in a long-running case linked to attempted prison escapes in the 1970s.

output.headline: UN chief says Gaza death toll of 25,000 is 'unacceptable'
output.trail: Gaza's health ministry says most of those killed are women and children, and that thousands more bodies may lie under the rubble.

output.trail: The head of the Norwegian Refugee Council is calling for a peace process to begin amid Gaza's 'almost unparalleled suffering', as new figures show nearly 70% of those killed are women and children.

output.trail: At least 21 people were killed when an Israeli-hit building fell in Gaza City, with rescue workers saying their search for dozens more is hampered by a lack of heavy machinery.

output.headline: Gaza aid workers mount one of history's largest rubble-clearance operations
output.trail: Aid workers face the delicate task of clearing 61m tonnes of rubble in Gaza, which conceals unexploded Israeli bombs and the remains of up to 10,000 people.

output.headline: Health experts voice concern over disease spread in Gaza, writes Devi Sridhar
output.trail: Health organisations are more worried about disease than at any point in the conflict, with a quarter of Gaza's population at risk of dying from outbreaks within a year, writes Devi Sridhar.

output.headline: G7 draws a red line against a full-scale Rafah operation
output.trail: G7 ministers have warned that a full-scale offensive in Gaza's southernmost city would be catastrophic for civilians there.

output.headline: Report finds Swiss glaciers lost a tenth of their volume in two years
output.trail: The volume lost during the hot summers of 2022 and 2023 equals the total depletion recorded between 1960 and 1990, a new report says.

output.headline: Eight years: that's how soon Alpine glacier loss could peak
output.trail: The climate crisis is forecast to wipe out thousands of glaciers a year globally, threatening water supplies and cultural heritage.

output.headline: Climate crisis made Spain's wildfire weather 20 times more likely, study finds
output.trail: A new study says global heating has made hot, dry and windy conditions in Spain at least 20 times more likely than before.

output.headline: 2,025 died during France's record June heatwave, officials say
output.trail: Public health authorities say the toll during the hottest week of the record June heatwave, a rise of 30%, is probably an underestimate, and expect it to rise further.

output.headline: Climate denial 'lies' must be rejected, says EU's Ribera
output.trail: Teresa Ribera says Europe's latest heatwave shows the need to reject climate denial, blaming 'ideologically driven' falsehoods, driven by those with vested interests in fossil fuels, for attacks on green policy.

output.headline: Annual monitoring tracks continued melt of world's glaciers at historic rates
output.trail: The latest results come even as some have cast doubt on claims that scientists have exaggerated the scale of glacier melt.

output.headline: Doctor's failure to find a vein halts Tennessee execution
output.trail: Tony Carruthers's lawyers say no evidence ties him to the 1994 crimes he was convicted of, and that he is mentally incompetent.

output.headline: Pike's lawyers ask supreme court to grant a stay of execution
output.trail: Tennessee is set to carry out the first execution of a woman in 200 years, after the governor denied Christa Pike, 50, clemency for the 1995 killing of a Knoxville classmate.

output.headline: Cities offered $300m in federal funds to copy Memphis-style policing
output.trail: The Department of Justice will give $300m for police enforcement surges across four cities, on condition they abandon what it calls progressive approaches to policing.

output.headline: Tupac Shakur murder trial opens in Las Vegas
output.trail: Lawyers have given a full account of the killing as the trial of Duane 'Keffe D' Davis, 63, a former South Side Compton Crips gang leader, opens, though some witnesses are refusing to testify.

output.headline: Mangione admits causing UnitedHealthcare CEO's death in federal plea
output.trail: The plea comes weeks before a separate case is scheduled to start in New York, and could throw those proceedings into disarray.

output.headline: Hines's lawyers ask supreme court to intervene before execution
output.trail: Darrell Hines's lawyers are asking the US supreme court to intervene, arguing he could face a fate similar to a botched execution attempt in May.

output.headline: Guide price set for Oasis archive despite band's legal objections
output.trail: An archive of concerts, rehearsals, soundchecks and conversations has been given a guide price of between £1.2m and £1.6m, despite the band's objections.

output.headline: Oasis to revisit the site of their greatest live triumph in 2027
output.trail: After 2025's wildly lucrative reunion, the Gallagher brothers will tour the UK, Ireland and US, revisiting the Hertfordshire site of their greatest live triumph 30 years on.

output.headline: Inside Don't Look Back in Anger: Oasis's biggest rockumentary of the year
output.trail: Capturing the band's 2025 global comeback tour, this two-hour film reveals the tense first rehearsal with Liam, a surprisingly soft-hearted Noel and the Gallaghers' politics, though don't expect any mention of ticket prices.

output.headline: How the Guardian missed Oasis's historic Knebworth 1996 gigs
output.trail: Noel Gallagher told fans 'this is history', but the paper opted to review support act the Charlatans instead, as that band returned from tragedy.

output.headline: Bucket hats and euphoria as Oasis open their Australian tour
output.trail: Bucket hats were out in force at Marvel Stadium as Liam and Noel Gallagher made a polished, and even affectionate, return to Melbourne.

output.headline: Noel Gallagher pulls out of Oasis's overseas tour
output.trail: The band's future looked precarious after the songwriter withdrew amid rumours of a rift with his brother Liam.

output.headline: What new academic research reveals about the Staffordshire hoard
output.trail: The first major academic study of the find suggests the 'war hoard' was probably captured in battles between regional kingdoms.

output.headline: Academic challenges assumptions about the Book of Kells' Iona origins
output.trail: An academic challenges the assumption that monks on Iona created the manuscript, arguing instead that its origins may be Pictish.

output.headline: Medieval tannery discovery astonishes experts at Fountains Abbey
output.trail: The discovery of the foundations of an 'industrial scale' medieval tannery at the abbey has astonished experts.

output.headline: Researchers recreate 16th-century choral sound using gaming technology
output.trail: Researchers have used gaming technology to capture how choral music would have sounded in the chapel at the birthplace of Mary Queen of Scots.

output.headline: Bake sales and sponsored walks help save Iona's historic abbey
output.trail: The Benedictine abbey on the Hebridean island reopens tomorrow after a £3m renovation funded by community fundraising, including bake sales and sponsored walks.

output.headline: Mystery royal stone head at Shaftesbury Abbey called 'absolutely stunning'
output.trail: An archaeologist describes the 'absolutely stunning' carved head, found at the abbey, as possibly representing Edward II.

output.headline: Signs of recovery emerge in England's tern colonies
output.trail: The National Trust says the latest figures are encouraging, with numbers of birds on the rise, though there is still work to be done.

output.headline: How local activists halted dredging and saved the Summer Isles' seas
output.trail: Local activists and small-scale fishers battled hard to protect their coastline, halting the scallop dredging that had been destroying the seabed as fish and shellfish populations fell rapidly.

output.headline: Australian electric car sales more than double to record levels
output.trail: A record 157,957 new EVs were sold nationally between January and June, equivalent to one every 100 seconds, according to the Electric Vehicle Council.

output.headline: Wetter, cooler weather may explain bogong moths' recent bump
output.trail: Wetter, cooler conditions are thought to be behind the moth's recent surge, after numbers dropped by up to 99.5% between 2017 and 2019.
output.progress: Experts advise on how to safely remove bogong moths from homes during the current influx.

output.headline: Sure Start principles underpin expansion of Healthy Babies scheme
output.trail: The programme will follow the principles of Sure Start, helping families with infant feeding, mental health support and bonding with their babies.

output.headline: Tsuda wins landmark Tokyo court case over AI voice cloning
output.trail: Tsuda won his case against a TikTok account that copied his 'lustrous' voice, in a landmark Japanese verdict protecting publicity rights.
